1225644_b04389b4.text: The overwhelming majority of these studies have focused on inputs to and projections from the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Relay neurons within dLGN receive strong glutamatergic inputs from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and serve as the principle conduit of visual signaling to the cortex. However, relay neurons do not act as passive relays of visual information. The gain of retinogeniculate signal transmission is modulated by nonretinal inputs to dLGN. These nonretinal inputs arise from visual cortex, pretectum, brainstem, thalamic reticular nuclei, and local dLGN interneurons, and they far outnumber the more powerful retinal inputs (Sherman et al., 2002)(Sherman, 2004). In fact, nonretinal inputs account for as much as 95% of the nerve terminals in dLGN (Sherman et al., 2002)(Erisir et al., 1997)(Erisir et al., 1997)(Horn et al., 2000)(Bickford et al., 2010)

1225644_3cdc4e87.text: .Retinal, cortical, brainstem and inhibitory nerve terminals in dLGN all contain distinct neurotransmitter synthesizing enzymes and synaptic vesicle associated transporter proteins necessary for their specific functions (Erişir et al., 1997)[7](Montero et al., 2004) (Gabbott et al., 2004)(Moore et al., 1993)(Fremeau et al., 2001)(Land et al., 2004). At the ultrastructural level, several types of nerve terminals have been described in dLGN, defined by anatomical features such as terminal morphology, synaptic vesicle shape, and mitochondrial appearance (Bickford et al., 2010)(Guillery, 2004)(Lund et al., 1972)(Robson et al., 1979)(Hamos et al., 1987). One set of nerve terminals contain flattened, oval shaped synaptic vesicles, a hallmark feature of inhibitory GABAergic terminals, and are therefore called F terminals (Sherman, 2004)(Lund et al., 1972)(Famiglietti, 1970). In dLGN, GABAergic terminals arise from the thalamic reticular nucleus and local inhibitory interneurons [7,18]19].

1225644_cc0d1672.text: In contrast to dLGN, which relays image-forming visual information to the primary visual cortex, vLGN and IGL contribute to functions of the non-image forming accessory visual system, such as irradiance detection, visuomotor responses, and circadian photo-entrainment [22,23].
